passage:
Dear Mrs Bhatt,

I'm writing because I can't say this out loud without crying. For about six weeks, Kamal has blocked me in the corridor outside the science lab and pushed my bag off my shoulder. He calls me names and the others laugh. I have told my mother I have a stomach ache four times so I don't have to come to school, but it isn't true. I feel sick when the bell rings. I used to think I must have done something to deserve it. I've started to believe that isn't true. I wrote down the dates: 3, 10 and 17 September, and yesterday. I stay near Anaya and Meher at break, and they don't laugh. Please can we talk after class on Monday? I'd rather not do this alone.

Arohi

Mrs Bhatt's reply, the same afternoon: Thank you for telling me, Arohi. This is not your fault. Stay after the last bell today and we'll see the counsellor together.

qa.q: For about how long has Kamal been blocking Arohi in the corridor?
qa.a: He has been doing it for about six weeks.

qa.q: What is Arohi feeling about school, and how do you know?
qa.a: Dread and fear. Arohi writes of feeling sick when the bell rings and of claiming stomach aches four times to avoid coming.

qa.q: What steps has Arohi taken that a wise person would suggest?
qa.a: Arohi wrote down the dates, stays near supportive friends at break and is asking the teacher for a talk instead of facing it alone.

qa.q: How might Mrs Bhatt feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably concerned and glad Arohi trusted her; she replies that same afternoon, says it is not Arohi's fault and arranges to see the counsellor together.

grounding: Arohi dreads the corridor and lies about being sick because of a bully, and writes to a trusted teacher with dates, staying near supportive friends.

passage:
Monday. Kashish told Mummy she had a stomach ache. It was the third Monday in a row. The truth was the corridor near the stairs, where three older girls waited every morning to knock her books down and call her names.
Wednesday. Kashish's friend Aditi caught her hiding in the library at break. "It's those girls, isn't it?" Kashish nodded, eyes stinging. Aditi didn't let it go. "We're telling Mrs Pillai. Now." In the staff room, Mrs Pillai listened to all of it. "This is not your fault, Kashish. Nobody should have to put up with this." She asked Kashish to write down dates and what happened, and she phoned Kashish's mother before the last bell.
Friday. Kashish walked to class with Aditi and two friends from the choir. A teacher now stood near the stairs every morning. The girls looked away. Kashish's stomach still fluttered, but she went to school.

qa.q: What did Kashish tell Mummy on Monday?
qa.a: That she had a stomach ache.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel about the corridor near the stairs?
qa.a: She felt dread and fear, enough to pretend she was sick three Mondays in a row.

qa.q: Which steps helped Kashish, and why?
qa.a: Aditi took her to a teacher the same day, Mrs Pillai listened and called her mother, Kashish noted the dates, and she stayed near supportive friends.

qa.q: How does Mrs Pillai see what has been happening to Kashish?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai sees it as serious bullying that isn't Kashish's fault, so she acts the same day and puts a teacher by the stairs.

grounding: A teen who dreads the corridor and pretends to be sick tells a trusted adult with a friend's help, notes dates and stays near supportive people.

passage:
Ramesh beta, you've been skipping school and saying you have a fever. Your mother told me. Let me tell you what happened to your Nazia Aunty at your age.
In Class 9, a group of boys in my school waited near the water tap every day. They pulled my dupatta, mocked my accent from the village. I started telling Ammi I had a headache, a stomach ache, anything. I thought I had to put up with it, that I somehow deserved it.
The turning point was my Hindi teacher, Mrs Sharma. She saw me eating lunch in the storeroom and asked why. I cried and told her everything. She said, "This is not your fault, and you do not have to bear it." She made me write the dates in a notebook, and she went to the principal that same afternoon.
After that I always walked with my friend Shobha. The boys were punished. And I finished school. So tell someone, beta. Today.

qa.q: Where did the boys wait every day?
How did young Nazia feel about going to school?
qa.a: She felt afraid and ashamed, even believing she deserved the bullying, so she pretended to be ill.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nazia Aunty's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Telling Mrs Sharma, who reassured her, had her note dates and went to the principal that day, turned hidden fear into adult action.

qa.q: How did Mrs Sharma see young Nazia's situation?
qa.a: Mrs Sharma saw it as bullying she should not bear, not something she deserved, and acted the same afternoon.

grounding: An elder recalls dreading school because of bullying, telling a trusted teacher, noting dates and staying near a friend.
